utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is Monday, September 3rd, and I welcome Mr. Stringer for Prosecution, counsels for Defence, and the accused in this room. We're now to continue the hearing on the cross-examination of this witness, but I think Mr. Kovacic has something to say first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. Good afternoon to the Trial Chamber and everybody in the courtroom. I apologise for taking two minutes of the Court's time but I just have to do so. On Thursday the Defence counsels discussed the situation. We analysed it and we came to the conclusion that, with the best will in the world, although that had been our intention that we simply don't have is enough time to prepare a response to the Prosecution's submission of the 27th of August requesting the introduction of 380 documents with respect to the military structure of the HVO. As the Trial Chamber already knows, we are working on seven similar requests by the Prosecution. There is 1.600 documents in all, and 45 statements, witness statements. The Trial Chamber also knows that we have limited resources, and so we cannot cater to such large amounts of material. We were given until the 8th of September to respond to the Prosecution motion, but since we have to respond to other motions as well between the 10th and 24th of September, with this additional amount on the table we came to the conclusion, Your Honour, quite simply that we could not do that. So we would like to ask you additional time, ideally until the 8th of October, but the normal deadline according to the rules would be the 10th of September. Now, in view of the other six motions we're working on, we fear that we simply don't have enough time. Most of the Defence teams worked during the weekend, and we just can't keep abreast with all this administrative material, so we ask for an extension in time. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough have, Your Honours. It is the request tabled by all the Defence teams, and the Trial Chamber has given us the instructions that we should all pool our resources when that is necessary and possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the floor to the Prosecution for its observations, but if I understood you well, this request deals with the Prosecution's submission on the submission of 380 documents dealing with the military structure of HVO. The deadline was September 10th. So you said there's a lot of work ahead of you. There's a lot of submissions. Many motions that you have to respond to and it seems you will not be able to make it by September 10th and you're asking for an extension until October 8. And this is a joint request for all Defence teams. So, Mr. Stringer, what do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has deliberated immediately and allows the motion presented by Mr. Kovacic given that Prosecution made no objection. Defence will have until October 8 to respond to the -- to the Prosecution's motion on the 398 documents dealing with the military structure of the HVO. So you have until October 8. Now, regarding the next witness, let's take stock of the time left. Mr. Praljak used up 78 minutes, and you have 42 minutes left. After this Mr. Prlic will have 30 minutes and Mr. Coric's Defence will have 30 minutes. According to the time. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have ceded our time to the Prlic Defence. We're not going to need to cross-examine this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, Mr. Coric's Defence time has been allotted to Mr. Prlic's Defence. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Tabeau. Your hearing will continue today and we will have the cross -- the rest of the cross-examinations and the redirect, and I will thus give the floor to General Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Because of the shortness of time once again could you please give me brief answers wherever possible. Of course, we don't have enough time to go through your very lengthy report, but anyway, would you turn to the portion where you speak about deaths or violent deaths in East Mostar. Page 10 of 32 pages. That is in the Croatian, of course, the Croatian translation. It's table 3. We've already mentioned that. It's page 7 of the English where you state that 373 cases fall within the relevancy test. And then I'd like to refer to the following Croatian page and table 4. Table 4 in the Croatian text. And in table 4 you give the month of death, the number of deaths in East Mostar, unknown causes in view of date and place. And April 1993, let's take a look at that and look at the 7th -- or, rather, July, August, and September where the number of both known and unknown deaths increases. Now, this disruption, disturbance, in the number of deaths according to the months and the observations you make here, do you know why under a siege, as you put it, there would be such a disruption in the distribution of deaths if we look at the months of the siege? Did you ever wonder why, why there was a disturbance or why there were differences, whereas the siege was an ongoing state?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't study the causes of the killing, so I can't say that I know why. Well, cause is general, I mean external factors, the siege activities. I'm not speaking of the causes of death as such.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. So you've never heard of something called Neretva 93 offensive?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what -- what is this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please turn to page 19 of the 32 pages. It's table number 10 and 11 -- or, rather, table 11. Let's look at table 11. Table 11. You say status of siege-related victims reported in the Mostar war hospital books. It's page 13 of the English.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the table.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And you state here that the victims, according to the Mostar war books as follows: There were 160 civilians, 12 detainees, and military 158, and unknown 142. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. Now, am I right in noticing once again in this instance that you didn't take the unknown into account when you calculated the percentages because the civilians, detainees and military you took as a sum, whereas you have left out the unknown. So it's 47. -- 47.9 per cent the military and 48.5 per cent civilian because you've left out the unknown; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the unknowns are left out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to look at table 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before table 15 let's move to -- let's stay on table 11. Here you have 12 detainees that are deceased, in table 11. So as far as the research that you've done, could you tell us whether you studied the situation of these 12 people? Were these people who were wounded when they were admitted into the hospital and then died because of their wounds, or are there other causes to their death? This figure of 12 appears here statistically so could you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't study these particular 12 cases. This can be done. We can check the record of these 12 persons, but I can't say what kind of cases are these 12 cases right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Page 26 of pages 32 -- or rather, table 15 is what I'd like to look at. It's page 17 of the English. The source. You have a sentence here that reads as follows: "Records of deaths which coincide with the records of fallen fighters means that they can be taken into account as soldiers, where as the rest can be taken to be civilians." So these records from the war hospital, did you compare that data from the data that you received from the Ministry of Defence about the killed in the BH army and then change the number of soldiers killed, the number of deaths? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did compare these records with the matched records, and there is a table in a -- in the report on the wounded persons which presents the results of this comparison. The table is unavailable from the report on the killed persons. There is a table in the report on the wounded persons to which we can refer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll deal with that in due course, but look at the remaining part of that sentence. And then you said the rest -- "And all remaining records as civilians." Is it true that you did not compare any other list of those -- of the deaths from the list of the armed forces, which means the civilian police as well, all the armed forces and civilian protection and everybody else helping the army? Quite simply, those who did not die as soldiers or militaries you termed civilians. So you say all the remaining are civilians without going in to see whether according to some other sources some more soldiers or militaries would be found; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I kept the original reporting of civilian military status available from the war hospital records. This is the most important thing. In the second step we matched both, war hospital records and also death registries with the military lists. From these lists we could see that a number of additional cases could be marked as militaries. We also saw that for a number of civilians reported in war hospital, the -- they were matched with the list of fallen soldiers. So we took the most conservative approach, and we remarked the civilians that were found in the military lists and took them as soldiers in the analysis. But -- this is what we have done, but your question is about whether we used any additional sources next to the sources I mentioned in my report to compare the -- the marking of the military/civilian status, and my answer is no other additional sources were used except for the military lists.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That seems satisfactory, because there are other sources of -- of course, too, such as profits for people who took part in the army remuneration, whatever. Certain advantages, at any rate. Now let's move on to your second topic, the number of wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before moving on to another topic, following your question, madam witness, this is absolutely essential for the Bench, this distinction between, on the one hand, the civilians, and the military on the other hand. If civilians were killed this will have consequences. We looked at the hospital record, the admission record, and you said that you worked with this record, and we have it as an annex. It's 2007 and 86, and obviously when somebody is wounded or killed there is something written in a column if this person has military status. However, it may occur that a civilian would be admitted into the hospital in civilian clothes even though it's a military person, because this person was on leave, for example, and changed clothes. But maybe this person was -- eventually got killed during combat because he's a military, but in the record here he will be listed as a civilian. Furthermore, when hospital notes that this person is a military status, it may be somebody who just as military clothes, in a military jacket, and that is why he is noted as being a military. He might just be a civilian who just wore a military jacket. We've seen evidence that has shown that sometimes civilians wore military clothes, and the opposite was also true. So when I was listening to the question and to your answer, a question came to my mind. I wondered whether you looked into the dates of birth of these people and whether you looked into the status of the able-bodied men, adult men, who according to law were considered as integrated into the armed forces when they were between 18 and 60. So if we take an assumption of a 45-year-old man wounded, who is suddenly wounded and is admitted into the war hospital in civilian clothes, what do you make of this man? Is he a military for you or is he a civilian? This is a very lengthy question. I apologise for this, but when you matched the data, did you look at the age of these people to be almost sure that in the tables when you note either civilian or military you also took that parameter into account, age, knowing that you haven't matched this with the listings of the ABiH, which according to the evidence presented by General Praljak seemed to prove that there were a great number of military in the 4th Corps who were killed. So did you first, did you -- did you take into account the age of the victims to make your distribution between civilians on the one hand and military on the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the short answer is no, we didn't look at the age as the criterion for the decision whether or not a person could be considered a military or not. Of course I have seen approaches based on age only. Basically speaking in this age-based approaches, men at military ages are all excluded from the list of civilians. There are, simply speaking, no men, disregarding the actual situation in which the person would die. Only women, all ages, and children, and the elderly or taken and placed on a list of civilians. We didn't follow this approach. Our approach was data driven. We had in one of the sources, war hospital, the military/civilian status available for a number of patients. This was the basis, the starting point for us in our analysis. We considered these cases for whom we had the status available as a subsample coming from a bigger sample of all war hospital records. And based on this subsample, we estimated the frequencies of civilians and militaries, reported civilians, and reported militaries. In the second step, we applied the subsample-based proportions of civilians and militaries to a larger list, the so-called master list of all victims and ended with an estimated number or numbers of civilians and militaries. That was method one. Method number two was also data driven but was based in addition to what was available in the war hospital, the reported status available from the war hospital books. We also included the results of matching of other sources with the military lists. From the matching we could have more information about the militaries, the persons reported as being killed as members of the army or certain other groups associated with the army. Well, this of course doesn't answer the question in what circumstances these persons were killed, whether a soldier in civilian clothes killed while being on a leave or perhaps a civilian having gone and fighting. This is not possible. This cannot be seen in the sources. The individual circumstances of every death cannot be seen in the sources. That is exactly the same with the age-based approach. Whatever we do with age, it is always some related resulting in some bias because not all men at military ages are combatants killed in combat and not all civilians -- not all civilians can be seen as civilians killed in non-combat situations. So all these approaches are, in some sense, deficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you for your answer. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, the second part of your analysis or your expert report, that's what I'd like to look at. Page 6 of the 60 pages of the entire report. That's the B/C/S. In English, it's probably a few pages before that. And it says here that some records were introduced or entered perhaps after -- after the person arrived, because the medical staff were too busy. Now, this term "too busy" and similar qualifications, I'll deal with that for a few moments. Let's see what was recorded at the war hospital. The identification number; the date the person was admitted; the surname; the year of birth; the status, civilian or military; the military unit at the time of the incident; the place of the incident; and how it occurred. So all these things should have been recorded. Was it -- were they indeed recorded in the war hospital records? Is that right? Were those the basic facts that had to be entered and recorded?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was looking for this table. You are saying it's page 6 in the B/C/S report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Four and 5 of the English. It's not a table. It just lists what was in the records, what should have been recorded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the death registries; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: ID given, first name, father's name, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Of the wounded. The wounded. We've moved on to discuss the wounded. Can you tell me whether it's correct that these are the records entered into the hospital books of the war hospital?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, indeed. On that page 4 and 5, English version of the report, there is a list of items that were registered for the wounded persons in the war hospital books.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. And in footnote 5 you then say that someone, native speakers of B/C/S, entered the sex, age, and nationality. You improved the list by getting some people to enter sex, age, and nationality. As forthright to change one's nationality, I won't go into that any further. We've already mentioned the case of the Yugoslavs and so on who had the right to declare themselves differently, but how do -- how did these people discover the age of the wounded? They had a book with 5 or 6.000 entries, and then they determined the age based on what? You can tell the gender by the name, but how do they know the age? If the doctors had on the average 14 patients and were so busy that they were unable to enter that information, they were unable to enter the details such as age, how did that be done subsequently? I'm really interested to know that.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the year of birth was reported for the patients in the books, and the age is calculated as a difference between the year of wounding and the year of birth. We do this in demography very often. We do it all the time. So not only the data entry clerks, the B/C/S native speakers did their own estimate of age. We did the same later by calculating the difference. And regarding ethnicity, I want to stress this is a study of sources reporting on -- reporting on Bosniak victims. So it wasn't a purpose of this study to include all victims of the siege. On the contrary. The purpose was -- I was tasked to prepare a report that would be summarising casualties among the Bosniak victims. This is why the war hospital books were used as a source representing these victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam -- I'm terribly sorry, Mr. Praljak. But Mr. Praljak raised an issue that triggered my curiosity on a particular point. This register, when we look at it very closely we can notice that it was a register that existed for the JNA, that was in the JNA army, because on column 6 you can see that we can see military rank, and there must be as well a reference to column number 5, which is military district of the person who was admitted. In fact, this register was enforced in the JNA. So one may think that this military hospital used this register in order to evaluate all this, but they did not take into account these various columns. Now, Mr. Praljak posed a very interesting question since he was asking you how were they able to know what the date of birth of the person was. If they put down the date of birth, that is either because the injured or the wounded person had his military papers on him or maybe because that person was identified subsequently. So my question is as follows: Did you and your colleagues look into the classification method that was used to admit people by using the criteria in the former JNA, or did you use -- do you think that they used it as a work tool without being particularly precise, without a great deal of precision, let's say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, regarding the JNA form which was used to register the patients, it is just what they had in the hospital. There is no link between this form and how and what was registered. In the siege of Sarajevo, for instance, one of the important sources was printed on the sandwich paper, because that was the only paper available, and we see the same -- exactly same situation here. This JNA, former registration of JNA members, these forms were just used because they were available. There was no other paper available. And the list of items I reported are the actual items reported in the books as such. I don't think that the method of registration was a very complicated one. These are all self-reported items as mentioned by the patients at the admission to those who were taking these records. So regarding the date of birth, it is just the reported date of birth or year of birth in most cases that is available. There is no documents underlying these answers. There is no military document that would tell us that the person was a military or a soldier. I hope I answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak, please proceed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, please turn to page 15, table number 5. Table number 5. My question is very simple. Or, rather, page 10 in the English text, table 5. And you say: "Cases treated in the war hospital according to indication of wounding." You say 2.549 are marked as wounded, and 2.844 are not marked as wounded. And two or three lines below you say the remaining 2.844 cases or 52.7 per cent of the cases were not marked as wounded, which means that in the books of the war hospital the diagnosis was not mentioned. And then a line below that you say that strictly speaking, 2.500 -- 2.549 persons could be counted in a strict approach as wounded, and you say this number is a minimum that has little to do with the reality of the siege. You said, just a little while ago, when I asked you why the distribution of deaths in those three months was different, you say that you did not deal with the war situation, and here, without any scholarly analysis, you say quite calmly that this number is a minimum that has little to do with the reality of the siege. This would imply that you were there during the siege and that you knew what it was like. So what was your scientific and scholarly basis for writing this sentence?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the basis for this is the source from which these records come. It is the war hospital books for approximately 2.500 of records, I have the diagnosis available and I could study this diagnosis. Among the cases available as you see, as you know, because I mentioned this, there is mention of shelling victims, gunshot victims, other violent victims. So that is my basis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, please. Do forgive me, but please try to be brief, because unless Their Honours grant me a little more time I won't be able to get through my questions. You say cases not marked as wounded, which means that in the books of the war hospital the diagnosis was not mentioned. You're accusing the doctors of not doing their job properly and then you take on their job and mark the diagnosis. I'm simply asking you on the basis of what scientific or scholarly foundation. The doctors did not enter the diagnosis and you say, I don't care because the siege and the war situation, which I'm not familiar with. I will say that these two groups are similar, the ones marked as wounded and those not marked as wounded. Just in a nutshell, please tell me do you have any grounds for this and, if so, what grounds, or do you not have any basis for this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have very good grounds. I'm extrapolating the results obtained for the patients with diagnosis available or with the patients with diagnosis unavailable, and my ground is an extensive study we completed of differences between these two groups: The group of patients with diagnosis and the group of patients without the diagnosis. As you see in the report, there is quite some room devoted to this issue. We test compared these two groups, separately for civilians and for soldiers using their age and sex distributions. We tested the differences statistically and the differences were not significant significantly, so there is no reason to believe that these two groups are different. Well, we tested the age and sex distribution because these are the basic demographic characteristics which, in this particular case, are responsible for human behaviour. If you have a woman and if you are age whatever but you are a woman, it is unlikely, highly unlikely that you can be seen as a military victim, as a combatant. If you are a man at military ages, then, well, it is much more likely that this death or wounding can be considered of a military person. So the sex and age differences between the patients with diagnosis and without the diagnosis are very important. And we studied them and tested them and the differences are, statistically speaking, insignificant. So there is no reason to believe that these two groups are -- ended in the hospital for totally different reasons, especially the timing of the arrival as patients was largely similar. So these are my reasons for my extrapolation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you say there is a set where the doctors entered a diagnosis, another set where the doctors did not enter any diagnosis, and you say that these two can be compared purely because there are some similarities in sex and so on, age and so on, as if there is no difference between the total number of the population and those who served in the army in this respect, but I won't go any further into this. Somebody else will deal with the clarity of this comparison of two totally different groups. I would now like to move on and go to page 17, table 8 or, rather, page 11 in your English original. That's table 8. And again we have internal definition of status and we have marked as wounded and not marked as wounded in the war hospital books. And again we have marked as wounded, civilians, 831. And not marked as wounded, 384 civilians. We have 29 detainees, 952 militaries, and 2.541 unknown. And then there is something that is unknown. Neither civilian nor detainee nor military but they are marked as wounded. That's a special subset. Some are marked as wounded, and they are neither civilians nor militaries nor detainees. What else is there? What other group is there, madam, in a town if you are dividing them into civilians and militaries and possibly detainees? Who are these unknown, and how did you arrive at this number of unknown? It is quite unclear to me how you came up with this number.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, you should be reading this table as a report on reporting problems in the source. It is -- unknowns are just cases for whom the status was unavailable; right? On one hand. But there was also another group for whom there is now two distributions, this two dimensional table, sir. You should see that in the last row, the unknown is relating to the status. So these are cases for whom the status was unknown. But for the cases for whom the status was unknown, there is a group of a number of them with diagnosis available, and this is 737. And the other group, 2.051 cases are the cases of unknown status for whom also the diagnosis was unavailable. This is a reporting issue. Obviously in this source there are many reporting issues and there are many unknowns or, say, unspecified categories. This is how you should be reading this table. And this section is summarising the problems in the source. This is not a section in which I discuss final results.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But would it not then be logical to have knowns and unknowns and then military, civilians, and so on, but this is mixing apples and oranges or do you know how many civilians wore military uniforms in Mostar simply because it was available and it was good quality and they had nothing else to wear? We have had witnesses here testifying to the fact that many civilians wore military clothes, and they would be then be the unknown who were wounded. Did you investigate that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an analysis of -- of the sources that were available to me which I am presenting here in this court. So I couldn't be making statements about things that I didn't study.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to page 19, table 10. In English it's page 13, table 10. And again you have external definition of status, marked as wounded. The number of civilians marked as wounded is now defined as 819. Civilians marked as wounded account for 819. Detainees, 23, and militaries, 1.006. And you say in this table very clearly that the number of civilians marked as wounded is 819. Is that what it says here, madam? You say quite clearly marked as wounded civilians, according to the war hospital records, 819. This is a clear, firm, precise number; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table summarises the results of -- of using the military lists in order to improve the reporting of the military status. So the number 819 can be compared with the number of -- from table, say, 10, can be compared with the number 831 from table 8.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it is lower number because certain cases were reassigned the status. And there was a small number of civilians that were also matched, as I said, with the military lists, and to be conservative we changed the status of these reported civilians into militaries because they were matched with the military lists. So this is how these two tables should be compared and should be read.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, madam, I've read that, and we have 92 as the number of soldiers. Is this table correct? Does it correctly show the real numbers you have available, improved according to the records of the war hospital? Can we consider this table to be true, correct, precise according to the war hospital books, improved according to your later checking of the lists from the Ministry of Defence which you received? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it is correct. As a result of the analysis that we completed for this particular part of the report, it's a correct table.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, madam. Now, please open page 22 of 60. It's probably some 2 pages further on in English. It says here in chapter 5: "I deal with the lack of availability of diagnosis and military status." Have you found this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You say the following: "The missing values are most probably the result of a failure to report woundings." So again you are dealing with somebody that is probably in your science probabilities marked by a number. So would you agree with me that probability theory with respect to a certain set or event is 5 per cent, 7 per cent, and that words such as "possibly," "very likely," and so on are avoided? So am I right in saying we don't know what "most probably" means here and that we can say here, for example, we can assume it could be assumed in the condition of?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking whether it can be measured, no. It cannot be measured in terms of a concrete number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Table 13, please. It's page 16 in English. That's another table that's important here. The sex patterns among marked and not marked as wounded are reported here, and was this table created by you or is it a correct table? Is it a created table?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean whether I made this table, then the answer is yes, I made this table.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But was it made according to the original data, or is it created according to the system of possibilities and so on? You can't answer that. It doesn't matter. But what I really want to know is: Is it correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. He did put a question to the witness and I think that she should be allowed to answer it. She was not given an opportunity. She was still waiting for the translation. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK:

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if your question is related to the sex that was originally not reported for many patients but was created on the basis of first names, so in this sense I can say the distribution is created in the sense that sex is not an item that is available for every single patient in the books.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Do you agree that mark of wounding, no, in that column the relation of men and women is 3.3:1, 630? That means 3.3 less women. And 3.8:1 is the ratio in favour of men with the mark of wounding. You can see that from your calculations of percentages. So do you agree with my calculation that there are approximately four times more men than women who were wounded?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see from the total in the first part of the table that there are 4.038 men versus 1.134 women.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, madam.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is 4 to 1 approximately. This is what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now -- now we're going to go on to page 37 of the 60 in the report and look at what is written underneath table 16. I'm going to read one of your sentences again. I'm not going to look at the table. We don't have time. You say, third line -- it's page 25 of the English. Third line from the bottom. "The percentages were obtained by including all the cases dealt with in the war hospital, adapted with statistical data regardless of the existence of diagnosis. Or, rather, disregarding the availability of their diagnosis. The estimates were obtained through including, in the adjusted statistics, all cases of treatments in or hospital, disregarding the availability of their diagnosis." Now, do you stand by that and that you included the rest in the system of further investigation regardless of the fact that no diagnosis existed?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to find this sentence you were reading, but generally I stand behind the fact that I made an estimate in relation to the absolute minimum number, and the estimate, the more complete minimum number included the cases without the diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now table 18b on the B/C/S page 39. It is page 27 of the English. Table 18b. Look at the distribution there. Minimum observed. That's what we know. You have men and women, and the total number of wounded militaries. Here we're dealing with militaries alone, soldiers. Judge Antonetti asked you what that distribution was. Now, does this show that from the ages of 20 to 44 you have double-digit numbers for the wounded or, rather, three-digit numbers for the wounded? And then the curve moves toward -- moves precipitously downwards when the older age groups appear, and younger ones, and that derivation curve is great. So is that right, what it says there?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is. There is figure 8, next page. So this is exactly what it shows.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we also observe that both women in that total number of 34 were wounded as members of the BH army or some other unit; is that correct? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are 34 women reported as militaries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now let's look at the last table. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can you tell me how much more time I have? I would need another 10 minutes to get through all this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think you have about eight or nine minutes left, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Maybe until the break perhaps so that I can complete my examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber is a bit skeptical. We'll take a break at half past. So you have 10 minutes to finish. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, take a look at table 22 now, please. It is page 46 in the B/C/S and 33 in the English. You have the wounding distribution according to place, locality. Can you in any way interpret this table? Can you interpret it, and do you know the military situation in Mostar? You already said you do not know or did not know. But what I want to ask you is the following: Those wounded in South Camp, in North Camp, you've divided them into three places. North Camp appears a number of times. So we have North Camp mentioned three times, three North Camps, one with 20 wounded, then North Camp again with 11 wounded, and then North Camp with 10 wounded. So North Camp is mentioned three times. Santiceva is mentioned twice. Why didn't you group all this together so that we have the right figure?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are the places as reported in the source. This is why we doesn't group them. We could have taken certain categories together. It was not a table that was meant to be interpreted and compared with any military actions in the area, but because these are the places with the largest numbers of wounding you can use this table in any other interpretation. So this report is not only meant to provide certain statistics for our --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well, fine.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- purpose but also can serve broader purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. You think that in analysing these data one should know whether in Santiceva Street, for example, there were any civilians at all for us to know what this is all about. For our interpretation we would have to know about the distribution of the units, whether there were civilians in Santiceva, in South Camp, North Camp, or whether they were purely military facilities; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't analyse this table from any other perspective, just by -- I did it to show the locations. So this is the actual contents of the source, no more purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, madam. I'm just asking you whether one would have to know that for further analysis. And my next question is as follows: Is it true and correct that in the 1992 population census this was done by 17.000 recorded census takers, 17.000 census takers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are not talking about the census right now. We are talking about war hospital records, and we are talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Doctor, we're not discussing this, talking about anything. I'm not your student. I am asking you the questions, and what I'm asking you is this: Do you know that more than 17.000 different handwritings for the record-takers are found working on the 1991 population census in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it comes probably from my report on the IDPs and refugees. There was approximately 17.000 interviewers who were taking the census records. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You could have said yes, that's right, without the explanations, because I have very little time, just five minutes. Is it true that the original population census records don't exist because they were burnt in a fire?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a new theory to me. I am unaware of any fire that would damage the census records.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, you can ask about that, receive information. Now, the second question. These records written down in different handwritings, and there's no subsequent checking of the material, do you know how many mistakes can occur in the optical record, alpha recorder, reader?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The census questionnaire was coded. It is not that every question was scanned as originally reported. Answers, responses were assigned numerical codes and those were scanned. And of course, the optical character scanning is not a perfect method and there are mistakes related to this. But how many? If you want a number from me, I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you. It wasn't scanned. This was introduced afterwards, and it was an optical scanner. So I'm asking you whether you know what the error rate can be and when you go on to correct the names and introduce them. So you put right the mistakes and you don't know how many of the records and facts were burnt. This is important data for data comparison. So do you know what is the error margin in percentages? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I can't express the error margin related to optical scanning as a number. I can't tell you how large is the error. I can only say errors are there and in every survey. It is in the census. Every other survey we have to deal with errors due to computerisation of the material. Whether it is optical scanning or it is data entry, there will be errors in any material, survey material that is computerised.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Doctor, madam, my question is a very simple one. You don't say there can be errors, will be errors, and so on. Do you know what the margin of error is? What is the possible error that one can make? Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, the witness has already answered the question. This is just an argument now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Maybe there's a misunderstanding. Mr. Praljak wants to know what is the error percentage. Can you answer what is the percentage of error possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, 100 per cent is the maximum error always. There can't be more than 100 per cent of errors. But I can't assess the percentage of error related to optical scanning. I can't assess this. I can't say. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, when entries are subsequently made, that people entered some facts on the basis of names, let's take a group of Serb names and then a Muslim group name and a Croatian name group. Now, can you give us the percentage where there is overlapping between Croats and Serbs and so on? How many names in common? How many names do you find in both groups? For example, in the Serbo-Croatian group. Take the Serbs and the Croats. How many names in common do they have or what is the cross-section of this group of names?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to object to the question. I believe it goes beyond the competence of this witness. She's testified that native speakers of the language are those who did the assessment of names and what ethnicities would be assigned names and that she didn't do any independent assessment of that on her own, so I believe the question is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, Mr. Stringer has just raised an objection. This witness told us that it is the native B/C/S speakers who allotted the ethnicity to the names, according to the names whether they were Serbs, Croats, or Muslims. It seems she has no knowledge of this. So she only took into account what others told her. And I think that's what you wanted her to say, whether there's a margin of error there. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is my basic question. The lady has signed other people's research, and on the basis of other people's research that she does not know about or cannot testify to their relevance, scholarly relevance, she goes on to compile a series of tables which I want to show are based on assumptions. Which, quite simply, don't stand scientifically. For example, Serbs and Croats, they have 50 per cent names in common. Slobodan is more a Serb name than it is a Croatian, so I would probably be ranked as a Serb voter or Serb refugee. I'm talking about the relevance of the expert team study. Because if you take over somebody else's data and information, you must stand by it if you haven't rejected it. And as another important group, although I don't have now more time, and that's the two groups in fact. One more minute may I have? It is a change data on the '91 census and the group of interviewees, voters, voluntary voters, that is to say, people who want to go to the elections. But I think Mr. Karnavas will address that issue further and I have completed my cross-examination. Thank you, madam. Through Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question after what Mr. Praljak said, please. Let's imagine that Mr. Praljak was admitted to the hospital because he was wounded. So he's wounded. He's admitted into the war hospital. His first name is Slobodan. If someone who has no idea who Mr. Slobodan Praljak might be, seeing this first name, which seems to be more common among the Serbs, could the conclusion drawn be that he was a Serb even though he's not a Serb? And out of this type of statement could you extrapolate the margin of error?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't do the assessment of ethnicity based on names, so I don't know what the others did, but if I was doing this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we've understood that you haven't done it. But you are responsible for this report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are testifying, not the B/C/S speakers. And the figures in your charts are based on these figures given by these B/C/S speakers. So any curious mind with a few mathematical or statistical knowledge might wonder and ask these questions, you know, whether out of a sample where consequences were drawn from the first name or the name in order to make the distribution, it would be interesting to know what the margin of error might be.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well there is quite a number of unknown cases, unknown on ethnicity, and I believe the -- this is my observation from the data that cases that were relatively straightforward for the B/C/S speakers doing the job were recorded as the Bosniaks. When it came to the cases that were obviously mixed cases like Slobodan Praljak, then these cases, most of them, were left like as unknowns. So this is not the case here that we have for every single record in the war hospital books ethnicity determined. We are not speaking of this situation. And I myself would behave exactly the same. So I would leave out a group of record of which I wouldn't be certain of ethnicity, just out. I would leave it out and not use it in -- in the analysis as determined cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we must now come to a close. One last question. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But, madam, you don't know about this, but anyway there are six of us here, and Serbs have the same first and last names. So with the Bosniaks the number is little less, but if you combine these names then you get 70 per cent. So that's what I'm asking you. Do you know this overlapping of names and what errors -- and this leads to errors and how much that error is when you have the same name in both groups, and then those errors are multiplied. That's what I'm asking you about, this margin of error and the number of errors in the census on the basis of these names.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am, of course, aware of overlap of names and that different ethnic groups may have the same names. And as I said, this can be studied in the census, and there is a whole distribution of ethnicities with the same names. But in most cases - this is my observation - there is a dominant group, the biggest group that is -- for which the -- a given name is typical. So in my view I can't say generally what is the margin error. If you are interested in a name, give me the name, and I will bring you the distribution tomorrow from my query in the census. That is so simple. It is a different margin for a different name. There is nothing like a common margin error for all names. There are names that are more common and more people are using these names and there are other names. We also know names, first, surname, that there is just one person having this name in the census. So it is very different depending on the name. This is why I cannot give an assessment for all of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And thank you, Your Honours. I regret that I cannot continue at least for another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We will now take a 20-minute break, and after the break Mr. Karnavas will take the floor on behalf of Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic is represented by Mr. Karnavas, and therefore Mr. Karnavas has the floor for the cross-examination. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. I would like to thank the Coric team for giving us the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just pick up where we left off with respect to margin of errors. There are all sorts of issues with respect to the margin of error that we can't identify in this particular case. For instance, what was the margin of error for the 1991 census. We don't know that, do we?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You know what the margin of error was for the results of the 1991 census? Say yes or no. What is your margin of error?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a yes and no question. Margin of error, if you think of coverage, well, census, was meant as a complete survey of the population, and I think this purpose has been largely achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the margin of error of all the names that you changed, you or your folks, because you're a member of the OTP, so we can't just pass the buck on to the others, but OTP members changed names. What was the margin of error of all the names that were changed to fit the formula of whether they fit into a Muslim, Serb or Croat? What is the margin of error?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not change to names to put into a Muslim, Croat, or Serb formula. We modified the names in order to eliminate spelling mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many names were modified; give me a figure?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I can give you if you give me time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. You had all the time to prepare. You testified on direct. You came here for cross-examination. Do you have a concrete figure that you can look in your report and say, that out of all of these numbers these are the number of names that we changed. Do you have that figure? Yes, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at hand. Can be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Is there a reason why it's not in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there a reason it's not in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we don't have it. We don't use it in any report. If you look through all my reports, you won't find this figure in any of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what was the margin of error of all the names that were changed; do you know? Or do you wish this Trial Chamber to assume and presume that every one of the changes was absolutely correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we speak of a misunderstanding. Changing the name, modifying a given name, has no impact on the reported ethnicity associated with this name. So there is no margin of error as all. Ethnicity remains the same for every name modified or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was some -- there was some discussion earlier on about certain names being similar, whether they're Serb or Croat or Muslim, and you indicated that your staff or the investigators, the B/C/S speakers, changed certain names because there were some problems with them.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is wrong. We haven't changed any names because there were some problems with them. I don't know what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What did you do, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We assigned ethnicity to the names reported in a source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what is the margin of error in the assignment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What is the margin of error, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Margin of error for which ethnicity was assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, what --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. My question is very precise.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a number. A single number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are overlapping again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be more than happy to spend two or three days with this witness. That's part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But it's certainly not helpful to make it all disappear because then you have no record. Better to have a record than none, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand and I appreciate the cautionary remarks from the Bench and from the translators. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what is your salary, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but this is not a question related to my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's a question that goes to your bias.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What is your --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Counsel wants to ask what her level is, we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But I think any greater specificity or disclosure on her part is not warranted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't see why this should be a secret. I'm a UN taxpayer. I mean, my -- my US taxes go to fund this place. I'm entitled to know, the public is entitled to know and it goes to the bias. If this woman was an employee of the OTP, has a high salary with benefits, obviously it goes to bias.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is unfair to ask any witness, while this is being broadcast over the internet, to tell the world what their level of salary is. Now, if we want to go into private session, counsel can ask what level she's employed at here within the Office of the Prosecutor. It's no secret and there's no dispute; she's an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor. And I think that really establishes the point right there. No greater detail is really required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Without asking any particular questions about the salary but, madam, all the employees of this Tribunal have either short-term contracts or long-term contracts, and they belong to a certain status, the P-1, P-2, P-3, P-4. Where do you belong exactly with regard to the P levels and the question posed by the Defence is not so relevant because the hierarchy shows the theoretical competencies of people, of employees. So somebody who is at a level P-5, for instance, has more, perhaps, theoretical knowledge than a person who is a P-2. So you tell us if you are a P-2, P-3, P-4, P-5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I still believe this is not an issue that should be discussed in the context of my report. This is not a secret but I would prefer not to speak about it but because I have been asked by you, I'm a P-3 and I have a fixed-term contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, does that also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you are a P-3. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does that mean you enjoy other benefit such as health care, pension? Are you into the pension plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you know very well that UN staff members have a certain status. There are certain rules. So it's a waste of time to ask this witness if she has pension benefits or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All we need to do is just read the documents that are available to all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Very well. Well, Your Honour, with all due respect, there is a difference if you are on a six-month contract or a one-year contract and you are on a contract that allows you to get rather generous benefits, pension benefits out of the UN, because, again, it goes to bias. This particular witness has worked for the Office of the Prosecution for several years, and I think that's one of reasons why I'm asking. So I -- it's a simple question. Is she, you know, vesting into the pension system. It calls for a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, again I object to the question. The witness has testified that she's been an OTP employee, she's done other reports, she's testified in other cases. We will stipulate, we will agree that she's been an OTP employee, that she's currently at the level of P-3, and that she has a contract that would give her all the benefits that a P-3 would be entitled to for a person having a contract greater than six months, and anything really further is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may say something. I am not entitled to all benefits because I'm employed here as a local person. I have right to have very good Dutch insurance for much less than the UN Van Breda insurance costs. And I have no benefits like tax-free purchasing and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, as I understand it, prior to -- this is the first time that demographers are being used in this context, and I'm speaking because of Mr. Brunborg, and during the Blagojevic case, he indicated that use of demographers by the OTP was an experiment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that, but what do you mean an experiment? There were posts created, two posts for professional demographers and still two demographers are employed by the OTP. I don't see it as an experiment any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Were the methods that you used and Brunborg used, were those methods used by other demographers prior to your employment with the OTP and prior to his employment with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the methods we use are not new and non-standard. There is one statistic and there are statistical methods. The context the method are used is new. I think it is for the first time that these kind of studies were made as the ones by Brunborg and myself, but also Patrick Ball made many reports of this kind in the context of other conflicts. It is not only the ICTY where these kind of studies that are made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the method you used, the methodology, the way that you took certain sources, the way that you cleaned up the sources, if I can use that term, the way you applied the sources thereafter, the matching or grafting, whatever you want to call it, that methodology, was that used with other conflicts, in other courtrooms in order to come up with some figure the way you folks have?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't think of other courtrooms but there were certainly reports made for truth commissions. Patrick Ball has made several these kind of records using the same methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The same methodology that you used?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Methodology you were referring to the matching methodology in the context of conflict studies. So my answer is yes. Outside this courtroom and this Tribunal, studies were made, but generally the methodology is not new. It's not non-standard. It's been years of experience in matching that we benefit from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a method that is used throughout many countries of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the manner in which you did the matching, that is a time-tested procedure?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's a yes or no, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not a yes or no question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, I'll withdraw the question?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question because obviously you don't wish to answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree, sir. I really want to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Then tell me: In the field of demography, what is the definition of siege?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no definition of siege within the field of demography and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about ethnic cleansing? What is the definition of ethnic cleansing within the field of demography as applied by your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there is a definition of ethnic cleansing in demography.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Whose idea was it, ma'am, to use the term "internally displaced persons" or "refugees," as you have done in your report, to identify people who moved within the country or moved outside the country, irrespective, irrespective of the reasons? Whose idea was it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose idea was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just used the term in order to make it clear that we are trying to statistically measure the displacement and we believe that is the best term to resemble this idea. Well, I wouldn't be able to tell you who figured out that this term should be used. We have been using this term since the very beginning of this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you say "we," who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We" is the demographic unit, and people who cooperate with this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that would be Brunborg who preceded you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I am part of the unit. And many people who worked in the unit throughout the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I read some of your articles, and in one article at least you talked about internal and external migration which is a rather neutral way of putting it. Why was it necessary to put in, to use the term, "internally displaced persons" or "refugees" especially when you do not give us a definition of how you're using those terms right up front?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason was as I explained. We tried to measure something that was a consequence of a conflict, and of course terms normally used in demography like "internal migration", "external migration" do not express the fact that certain consequences were related to the conflict. So the reason was we wanted to express the demographic consequences of a conflict the best we could and this is why we used the term. And secondly, I disagree there is no definition in my report, what I mean by internal displacement or migration -- well, refugees. There is a definition and we discuss this definition here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which page is it on, ma'am, because I notice -- before you answer that question, I notice that you have the presence of mind in your topic -- we're speaking of the second report, P 09836 titled "Ethnic Composition, Internally Displaced Persons and Refugees". There is a footnote. So you had the presence of mind to put a footnote there but it's not until, I believe, it's page 10 or 11 that you finally get around to telling us how you interpret or how you're going to use these terms. Was there a reason why you couldn't put your definition right up front and say that these are not normative terms, these are not terms as they're normally used in the courtrooms, but these are terms that we decided to use for convenient purposes?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is page 11 indeed where we explain what's our definition of internally displaced persons and refugees, and we explicitly say these are statistical definitions and no legal definitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, ma'am. Now with respect to siege, what is your definition of siege, number one. I'm asking a compound question but number two, how is it that you determined, you the demographer, that indeed what was happening in Mostar at that conflict, it was a siege or was this something that you decided to use, sort of, for convenient purposes?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't use it for convenient purposes. I rather follow the common definition, definition, or common use, say better. Well, in many press reports, videos, from this period the term "siege" is used and there is no other connotations behind my use this term. I just took it from the common use in the media in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, I take it you believe what you read in the media?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a yes and no question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, very well.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The quality of information in the media is very different, very very different, and there is no reason to trust everything you hear in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there anything in your report where you qualify the term "siege" or "ethnic cleansing" to suggest, at least to the Court, trying to be an objective and impartial and an independent expert, that you are using these terms merely because this is something that you read in the press, versus, say, the impression that I got from reading your report that you believed that there was a siege and that there was ethnic cleansing? Is there anywhere in your report where you -- where you alert the reader as to your intentions behind using these particular terms?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is no definitions of the terms "siege" and "ethnic cleansing," you are right. There is no definitions as such. But -- well, I am surprised you are talking about it as the ethnic cleansing is a term that has been used also in many legal documents in the Statute of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Really?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, really it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is a crime called ethnic cleansing, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, there is no definition in my report. Are you happy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you would agree with me, ma'am, that it's not your job to determine whether ethnic cleansing occurred, assuming that it did happen and we know what it is, or that a siege was taking place. That is not your job. Your job is to deal with figures and statistics; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but as far as I remember I didn't make any - in my final conclusions - any statements related to the fact that there has been ethnic cleansing, there has been siege and what is the meaning of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my final conclusions, I speak of the numbers and statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay very well. Now, getting back to your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Getting to your -- to your work the way I see it, and help me out here if I'm wrong, you know, we need to look at three basic things or the Trial Chamber needs to look at three basic things, one are the sources that you used; two, the methodology; and then three, the analysis or the interpretation of the results of that. Is that -- am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, speaking of the sources, we know that basically you're using, with this particular report, I'm sticking with this one since General Praljak covered the other two, you -- you rely primarily on two sources. One was the 1991 census and the other one was the voter registration in 1997, 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, primarily, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And now let's speak a little bit about the sources. Both sources have their limitations; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's why I asked initially if you could tell us the margin of error with the 1991 census, but let's talk a little bit about that. The data that you got from the 1991 census somebody else had prepared?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And prior to the 1991 census there was an effort in the former Yugoslavia to figure out how many households there were and how many members within these households; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably several attempts. It is the task of every statistical office in every country to have this kind of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] 1991, just stick with me, ma'am, work with me here, will you? 1991, that was the purpose of the 1991 census; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Part of it was related to households.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The purpose of it was not to measure how many Muslims or how many Yugoslavs or how many Serbs, Croats, or Montenegrins. That wasn't the real purpose behind the census, was it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the main purpose of every census in every country is to provide the count of the population. That is the major purpose but of course much more information is collected than just the number of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't ask what information was collected, ma'am. The purpose -- I'll move on. Let's stick a little bit with the issue of nationality. That's a subjective criteria, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a self-perceived item in the census questionnaire. It is self-perception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And anybody could answer it however they wished?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there was no way of checking that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by checking? Self-perception and responses are just the way things are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. So somebody could be, say, for instance, Montenegrin and claim to be a Serb. And there's no way to verify whether that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the person sees himself or herself as a Serb then it is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please do not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, there was no -- prior to the census, there was no testing done in advance; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, you are wrong. There was a pilot census in 1988 [Realtime transcript read in error "1998"].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Because you were asked about that, I believe in the Stakic case and at that point you did not know that. So I take it --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have not. I can't exclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So as of 2001 you weren't aware that there was a pilot project?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
