utterances.text: Well, I would be surprised at that time if there was no pilot census, because it's normally done. But I might at that time not know exactly about the pilot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Just as you did not know when you testified in Simic that there were international standards. That had to be pointed out to you in Simic, but then by Stakic you learned that there were indeed international standards?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is not correct. I am aware of the existence of international standards for large surveys like the population census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That wasn't your answer in Simic though; was it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know better than me. I can't confirm. I testified many times. I can't remember every testimony and every transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you check -- take a look and check the results of the pilot project?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself, no, I didn't. This was the role that -- of the authorities preparing the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, just a clarification. The record indicates, just on line 24, moving up that the pilot census was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: 88, 88 of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I wasn't sure if that was correct or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please do not overlap for the record. Thank you. And speak one at a time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when did you learn, when did you learn that there was this pilot census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I requested at some point specific reports about the preparations of the 1991 census from statistical authorities in Sarajevo. When exactly was it? It was probably around 2002, I believe. I am not sure that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. By 2002 how many reports had you -- had you used where you relied on the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I have been working with the population census since the time I arrived here. That is September 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am, how many reports did you write? I mean, it's a pretty simple question. How many reports?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably just one but we can check this in my --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I believe, sir. I don't remember exactly the dates of all my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were that many that I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, I don't want to waste my time on that. After the census was conducted --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see just one - sorry to disrupt you - in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, and that was which one?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, two. That would be two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because you testified in Stakic and it was pointed out to you and learned after Stakic. Simic comes before Stakic, so of course, there's two.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But do you find it wrong that I learned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is better that I learned --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- than I didn't; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am, I hope that this is not a trial-and-error process. You come into court, you learn in court and then afterwards, after you've done the damage, then you go back and try to correct it. I hope that's not the process.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish it is not as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after the -- after the census was conducted, normally there's also some sort of a post-data-gathering process that's normally done with the census to make sure that it's -- it's correct. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in this case, the 1991 census, that wasn't done?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done. There was a control census after the census. Actually, directly, even, after the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it is discussed in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, so as far as you know, it was done?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And is that why you put in one of your articles that it was done at the municipal level, they -- I believe you stated something to the effect that the municipal authorities cleaned up -- up. I have it right here. You indicate in one of your articles that the municipal census commission searched for and eliminated the duplicates within municipalities. That's on 200 and 201 of your article, one of your articles that you wrote and I'll get the title of it right now. "War related deaths in 1992 - 1995". That was published in the European Journal of Population, 2005.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, is it your understanding, really -- it's 1D 01658. It must be in your packet. That's what I'm referring to. I just want to pin you down here, ma'am. Is it your testimony under oath -- could you please help. Is it your testimony under oath, ma'am, that the municipal commissions searched for and eliminated the duplicates within the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please refer to the article where I'm discussing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes it's on page 200, 201. Let's me just ask you the question though. Is it your understanding that the municipal census commissions eliminated duplicates within the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but this is different than the control census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going step-by-step. Okay? So where there were duplicates before -- and then you say in your article in the next step the republican statistical office was supposed to clean up the duplicates observed between the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. May I ask where did you learn this information?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you would go through the report of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am, just kindly answer my question. If you would like for us to get a translator to speak in your native tongue, I can make that request. Otherwise, kindly answer my question. Where did you learn this information?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the report by Nora Selimovic, included as part of my report on the IDPs and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware there was an organisational manual concerning the census; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean like guidelines for interviewers, for municipal commissions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- For instructors?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, an organisational manual at the federal level, at the republican level, as far as what to do with the data once it was gathered? Were you aware that there was such a manual? I'm asking the question. Yes or no. Or in the alternative, were you merely relying on this person who you claim was an expert on the census, the B/C/S person?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the organisation of the census and conduct of census, there was census law. With regard to data processing and preparation of the publications based on census data, there, of course, this is part of regular work of every statistical office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, hold it.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So for this they don't know -- they don't need manuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, I just want to make sure I understand you correctly. What you're stating is: Either a manual does not exist, or you do not know whether one exists, a manual, that is, with respect to how to process and analyse the data after the census. And let me make sure that we're clear. I am not speaking about publishing the raw data as it was done sometime thereafter in an official publication. Those are two different issues. Are you aware whether there was an organisational manual? Yes, no, I don't know, I can't remember?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of these three answers that fits here because I am aware of several documents with several types of guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also for post-census data processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you can find all this in my report and in Nora Selimovic's report. I'm not exactly sure what you are talking about, organisational manual. I wouldn't really know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I explained it.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: About what? What should be regulated about this manual?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I don't want to overlap. I am told that, at least at the municipal level, the municipal census commissions as you stated could absolutely do nothing with respect to eliminate duplicates. All they could do is send the raw data and it was at the republican level that that would be cleaned up. Because after all how can one, as you put it, how can one municipal census commission determine the duplicates within another municipal census commission or municipal census data, if they don't have all of that? So according to you, the municipalities are trying to search for and eliminate duplicates from the municipality, and after that they send all this material to the republican level?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't get it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipalities, there were municipal census commissions. In every municipality there was a municipal census commission, and there was a group, interviewers and instructors, census instructors, who were jointly responsible for providing a complete material. "Complete" means that the coverage of a given municipality would be full, that there wouldn't be any households left out, not covered by the census, and in order to ensure that the completeness of the census, interview census commissions, municipal census commissions, and the interviewers received specific maps of the enumeration areas. Based on these maps, they were first of all supposed to check every household that was located in their areas and at the end of the census when they were providing their interviewers their materials to the municipal instructors, the instructors were obliged to collect the completeness of the questionnaires collected by the interviewers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And of course, the municipal census commissions had to approve this information and had to make sure that the completeness is assured, and at the same time, it was their role to assure that none of the households is counted twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. This is what --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within -- within the given municipality, of course. This is the municipal checks of the completeness and of duplicates --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the census response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me just read here what you say on page 200 of your article which you authored. At the bottom of 200, going to 201, you say, "Duplicates are not unusual in statistical surveys and therefore, during the 1991 census in Bosnia, this problem received the necessary attention too, and thus the municipal census commissions searched for and eliminated the duplicates within municipalities." This is what you state. Now, you stand behind that statement.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. "In the next step the republican statistical office was supposed to clean the duplicates observed between municipalities." So in other words, before the municipalities send the raw data to the republican statistical office, it is your belief that at the municipal level, they were eliminating the duplicates.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Within the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the municipalities by comparing the enumeration areas and the collected questionnaires and checking whether the households reported within the municipalities were not reported twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, very well. And the 1991 census was never officially certified because of the break-up of the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need to certify a census, as such. How do you think it is done?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it's your understanding that under the law that they had passed prior to the census on how the census should be conducted, the criteria, what -- how -- how to analyse the data. It is your understanding that it did not provide for some sort of final certification process?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just answer my question, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not a yes or no question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. There was a census law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the question is very clear and very precise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me restate it.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me restate it for you. Kindly listen to my question. Is it your testimony, under oath, that the law and the procedures set forth for the 1991 census did not call for some sort of end -- end-of-the-process certification by the official authorities? It's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law, census law, requested the authorities, statistical authority, for providing reports on the conduct of the census, including the financial aspects of the conduct, and such reports were provided to the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina as requested and were never disapproved. So do you think that there is a need of a special law which would say that the reports were -- have been approved? They were never rejected. They were never disapproved. It is not enough as a certification?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am, could you give me the actual number of all the duplicates that were ultimately found by the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the municipalities, you mean? Oh, I can't give you this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I'm saying for the entire census. Could you give me that figure?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I can't give you this figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that census data in my office; right? And not the study they made, the analysis, the cleaning they made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you're telling us, if I understand you correctly, that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they did a final analysis and they came up with a concrete figure of these are the duplicates. This is the number of duplicates. Can we see that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every municipality they probably have this figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You say probably, ma'am, I don't mean to overlap.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You see -- excuse me. You know, Mark Twain popularised a saying that was coined by Benjamin Disraeli, who as we all know was one of the greatest prime ministers of the UK, and Benjamin Disraeli said, you know, "There are three kinds of lies. Lies, damn lies, and statistics." Now we're dealing with an area called statistics because demographics is based on statistics. And that's why I'm asking you these very precise questions. So kindly answer my questions. Are you aware whether Bosnia-Herzegovina had a figure that said this is the number of duplicates? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unaware of this figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you come up with a particular number as to how many duplicates were within Bosnia-Herzegovina in the census? Did you, your office, your staff, OTP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes we did some checks for duplicates and came up with a number. I don't exactly remember, but it is in my article, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now when you say "some," does that mean you did a sample or you looked at all of them?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We look throughout all of the census records.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so you have a concrete number.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's several thousand duplicated records.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, several thousands well, several thousands could be 3, 6, 5, 10, could be 20. Do you have an exact number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will try to find this number for you right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And tell me also while you're looking at it, does that number -- is that number the raw number, or is it the number that you and your staff cleaned up as a result of trying to figure out the names and the nationalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't find it right now but I'm pretty sure it is here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could answer my last question?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in the range of, say, 8.000 duplicated records.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Eight thousand?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance, the figure of 8.500 can be found at the end of the first paragraph on page 201.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, does that figure include -- that's the one that -- does this number include duplicates that were -- let me rephrase it. In arriving at this number, is this after the raw data was checked by the B/C/S folks working with the investigative unit and you and were able to eliminate certain names?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well. I want to clarify. We used three different methods to correct the spelling mistakes in the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only B/C/S native speakers who were studying the names, but also, for instance, household method that was a search within household for one correct name and if such a name was found such a name was assigned to all other members of the household.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this method was very efficient in improving the spelling mistakes and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the duplicates were checked after the names had been cleaned from the spelling mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now you say the spelling mistakes were -- were corrected. As I understand it, there were folks that went household to household, sat there and filled out this data. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So presumably whoever was talking to whomever was spelling their names; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were just giving the names and the interviewers were writing them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then -- and then somehow your office decided that there were misspellings and therefore someone employed by the Office of the Prosecution decided to come up with correct spelling of these particular names?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me what the margin of error in that process is?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't understand what is the error here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, are you saying that every single one that was corrected is absolutely accurate?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether for each one that was corrected, assuming that it was an address, that it was checked to make sure that that person was the name reflected now that it was corrected with the spelling? Was any checking done?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was the checking done, ma'am? Did anybody go back into the field?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Not after our corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, now, when you corrected those names, did you send those -- that data to the official authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so at least officially they could look at it to see whether indeed what you had done, you and the others, on behalf of the Office of the Prosecution, could be checked and verified and maybe given -- maybe even given some sort of imprimatur by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not as such, not for the purpose of comparing and telling us what is the error made, but on several occasions samples of the data were returned to authorities in Bosnia, and we requested that these names would be checked in context of other sources reporting on the same persons, and surprisingly perhaps for you, not for me, but we received quite many confirmations related to the corrected names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it all of that information is available so if my expert wants to check all of that to see how many actually you sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina and what their responses were, I would be able to -- my expert would be able to verify that information?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was done on several occasions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- throughout all these years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am, ma'am, please, I kindly beg you to answer my question only.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you didn't listen to my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it says -- you could say yes. She's welcome to come, she could look at the data. You could say that.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your expert is always welcome to come. I will make anything accessible to your expert. I have no secrets but I told you that I didn't send samples with corrected names to statistical authorities to compare with the actual census questionnaires. I said it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay I --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- A few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand and I listen very carefully and I -- obviously you did not send --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- all of the names you corrected. Okay that's number one. Number two, the ones that you did send, do you have that data available? In other words, I would know that this list of names were sent to Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the authorities, and then they came back with some sort of affirmation or something verifying your work product. Is that information available?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It would be available if your expert would like to study --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's available?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but do you understand what you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. I'm just asking the question, ma'am, that's all.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's no need to read into my questions; they're pretty simple. All right. Now with respect to -- I don't have too much time to go into all the problems with the sources, but I want to talk a little bit about your choice between 1991, and 1997/1998, and I take it and this is no disrespect to you or criticism, but basically you -- you -- you dealt with the sort of sources that were available; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is -- if you are talking about 1997/8, I believe that the voters registers is the best source that can be used, and available. And it is available, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe I am just tired and I'm not phrasing my questions correctly. You have no data for 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No data for 1993?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just answer my question, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't have data for 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you do have this 1997/1998, and that source also has its own limitations; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again, we don't have that much time, but now, let me break it down even more. For 1991 prior to the outbreak of the conflict you don't know -- you don't have any statistics as to how many folks, for instance, might have participated in the census but left Bosnia-Herzegovina for whatever reason, employment, education, you know, whatever the reason might be. You don't have any data for that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, prior, yes, we do. This is part of the census questionnaire, the presence or absence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at the moment of the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this can -- this is reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, please, listen to my question. They're not trick questions. After the census, okay, somebody -- and incidentally, speaking of the census there were folks that filled out those forms that were living abroad; correct? You're shaking --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you don't know the actual reasons why those folks were living abroad, do you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is a reason reported in the census questionnaire but not after the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not after the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you have a concrete figure of how many people participated in the census but then left, say, in 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994 that had nothing to do with the conflict? Do you have any figures?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no figures at all throughout all these years, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So as you sit here - and I'm not being critical, I'm just merely trying to establish certain points - you don't know how many people during that period -- and the reason I picked 1991 to 1994 is because that's the period of the indictment. Okay?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you don't know how many people left voluntarily, do you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You don't know how many of those people left because, for instance, they had employment opportunities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or for instance, perhaps some could see that perhaps the situation was unraveling and there might be a conflict and so they left in advance and it had nothing to do with being ethnically cleansed but merely they had options and they chose to exercise those options; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you could say the same for 1992, 1993, 1994,; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now speak of 1995/1996 -- I have to slow down a little bit. We'll give the -- I picked 1995 because of the Dayton Peace Accords although we also have 1994, which is the -- the Washington Agreement, but for 1995 and thereafter, you have no statistics as far as how many folks decided to stay where they were because simply they wanted to be where they were, because the quality of life was much better than going back to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have some statistics by UNHCR on refugees, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when we talk about refugees, again you just told me that for 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, you can't tell me concretely how many people left or even moved within Bosnia-Herzegovina because they were exercising their own free will versus those who actually were chased out. Now, my question is: 1995 and thereafter, you do not have any concrete information, not just you, or anyone else for that matter, as to how many folks found themselves in the United States, Australia, Canada, Switzerland, Norway, Sweden, whatever, who had left for instance because of educational or employment opportunities, or because they left because of the war, because they had to, and simply did not want to return because now they had established themselves someplace else. You don't have a figure for that, do you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And again, I'm not being critical of you. It's just those are the facts of life; okay? Now, with respect to the movements there was a question by Judge Trechsel with respect to whether, you know, how many people were moving in and about Yugoslavia and maybe outside of Yugoslavia prior to the war and whether we could make some comparison. Do you know, you know, it calls for a yes or no answer, do you know whether there's any statistical data that would demonstrate 1991 or, say, 1981 and up to 1991 what was the movement within Yugoslavia, internal migration? Are there figures?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually brought a publication for Bosnia, and I have prepared some statistics, so any time we can discuss this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am, you can help me out here. Does that mean yes?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. And I take it in those -- they would reflect the reasons why somebody's moving, say, for instance, Serbia and now, they're going to, say, Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I brought figures for Bosnia, as I said, and you will see internal migration there, even within municipalities, and you will see external migration as well. That means into other countries. I believe other regions in republics, former republics --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- would be considered to be at that time still one the same country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And at that time there was no war?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 1991 statistics, so at the time no war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay it would be fair to say, and maybe this is outside the field of demographics, but it would be fair to say that when there is a conflict, at least some people who have options decide to get out of the way of harm, get out of harm's way; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Has nothing to do with ethnic cleansing. It simply has to do with wanting to go someplace where the family, the children can be safe; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really because as you know, ethnic cleansing --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hold on. Just listen to my question because --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very strong push factor. Let me finish; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we know it from Bosnia and we know it from Rwanda as well, so it is for whatever reason, conflict as such, conflict as such is a push factor for people to move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So don't say --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Some are moving out either before the conflict comes, when they know it's coming. Some may be leaving during the conflict, even though the conflict hasn't arrived at their particular municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let me just, because my time is running out a little bit, were you aware of the law that existed in Bosnia, it's called, I believe, the law on return of abandoned property. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware, ma'am, that part of the 1995 Dayton Accords call for anybody within Bosnia-Herzegovina, they could remain wherever they wished. They could remain where they found themselves in 1995 or go back to their place of birth or where they were prior to the conflict or move someplace else. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly. I didn't study this, but I am aware of the existence of the International Commission for Real Property in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But let me -- help me out here?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So they probably know everything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What if I were to tell you that, and this can be checked out, the Office of the High Representative was overlooking and still overlooks Bosnia and Herzegovina, but part of the Dayton Accords was that people could settle where they were or move about. In other words, there was freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't know simply --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if there is such a law you are saying so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now what if I were to also tell you -- or let me ask you this: Was abandoned property -- as folks were abandoning their property and moving elsewhere, were you aware whether that abandoned property was used by other, say, refugees coming in to those areas?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can imagine this property could be used by --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- others that lost their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware that the Office of the High Representative that was overseeing this, and there was an Ombudsman's office as well dealing with property issues, but were you aware that the policy then, post-Dayton, that folks that were occupying somebody else's residence would not simply be evicted but there was a need to find alternative housing if those individuals chose to remain in that particular location; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I can imagine this could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you have no statistics.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have the statistics but there is the CRPC, and I believe they have the statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what I'm driving at is: Let's say folks want to go back into a particular area but now their abandoned property is being occupied by other refugees. Do you know whether - we don't have a figure - how many people chose not to go back to their abandoned properties simply because there was no available housing, say, as late as 1997, 1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I have no statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if you look at the UNHCR statistics on internal displacement there was a high increase in the years 1997-8 because there were returns and people were unable to return to their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because others were occupying them.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others were occupying or houses were damaged. They were -- they had no place to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so we don't have those figures of how many people -- for instance, we can't say that a certain amount of folks chose not to go back to their place of residence because there was no housing available, not because they were being kept out, but simply there was no housing available and under the OHR policy and under the Dayton Accords folks could remain wherever they found themselves or wherever they wished.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the figures but I'm sure you can obtain these figures from authorities in Bosnia. These figures must be available, I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just because -- I'm asking the question because you as a demographer I would suspect to have known that, that perhaps when you look at the raw data, if you're going to go to that step of making a sort of legal or political statement that there is ethnic cleansing here, one would at least have some data to show whether indeed the low return was as a result of people actually not being able to come back because there's no housing available, or they don't want to go back because now the demographic has changed to the point that they don't feel safer any more. And we don't have that sort of data, do we?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but what's your question actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said several times I don't have the statistics on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's all that I want. I just want an admission on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, how much time do I have left? I'm moving around. I understand that it's not fluid, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, how much time do we have left? You have nine or 10 minutes more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With your indulgence if I could take 30 seconds to look at my notes to see what I could possibly do in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With the voters registration list, going back to that, that was the only available source post 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of this scale, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just to be sure, help me out here, that was -- people volunteered actually to registered, to register to vote; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It wasn't mandatory.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's not the sort of source that one could look at a demographer would normally look at; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in this particular -- this particular source also had some limitations; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One of the limitations was that, for instance, if we're trying to determine ethnicity, for instance, the voters were not required and indeed did not indicate their ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ethnicity wasn't available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we know that prior to -- prior to the conflict, at least when the 1991 census was done, I believe there were 29 different ways that one could describe themselves?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 91 ways.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what we see in the census results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I was told differently but 91. And just out of curiosity, there were ciphers or I think that's how it's called like a number. So a Croat would be, say, a 1, a Serb a 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, name, categories, but then combination of categories, regional groups, other nations, et cetera. Yugoslavs, of course, and some unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And some unknown. All right. And it's your understanding that in those combinations that were provided in the census I just want to -- I just want you to -- a clarification, they even had combinations Serbo-Croat, Croat Serb, a Croat Muslim. They had those combinations and they could sort of write in a number that would denote that particular combination. That's your understanding?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is now it was reported, yes, combinations are examples of those you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, when you say this is how it was reported, I'm asking whether the forms provided that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now the voter registration didn't provide any of that; right? One did --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by this point of course we no longer have Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now they're Bosniaks. Right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Bosniaks were also reported in the census so it is not that it was invented after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't say that it was invented, ma'am, and I'm not trying to go there. What I'm saying is that after this -- that we don't have that any more now in 1997/1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the voters, generally there is no ethnicity reported as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, the reason I'm asking however is at some point you're trying to go backwards and trying match names because you don't have all this other data, and that's the best that you can do?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, one of the things that we -- that you did have was a particular identification number that everybody was supposed to have; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that was the -- it's got this -- I think it's maticni broj or something like that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, help me out here. As I understand it, that had 13 numbers; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The first seven numbers were the date of birth?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the other six were sort of personal numbers.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some codes. Like sex was coded, region was coded, and within each sex there was a subsequent number issued to the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But those were -- those were personal numbers basically?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And not everybody had a maticni broj. Not everyone had that, right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a percentage of individuals who didn't report the number in the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Hold on. There's a difference between reporting it and not having it. When the 1991 census was done not everyone had one; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. Not everybody had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A small fraction didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say a small fraction --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 20 per cent say approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or I'm wrong. 13 per cent. Now I remember better, sorry.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So say between 13 and 20 and we can check it later and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the same thing when -- when people were registering to vote, one of the things that they were supposed to do was also provide this identification number; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the thing is that for the registration of voters the actual census data were used including the maticni broj and the names of the individuals. So it was, strictly speaking, the same electronic material that we have in our office that was also used for the registration of voters and is available in the electronic lists of voters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, in the -- in the previous case that I -- I employed an expert to look into this and had in fact had access to your data, apparently in BiH, in the BiH census, and this was as of 2004 when those figures were checked, 1.402.099 inhabitants, which would have been about 32 per cent of the total population of BiH which was 4.4, had an incomplete -- I guess they call it -- the short term is JMBG number. Would that being correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That might be correct. I don't remember the numbers exactly but some people didn't, some had incorrect, but the point is that exactly the same numbers were listed on one hand in the census material, and on the other hand in the voters registers, so it really doesn't matter if a number is correct or not because if you do the matching through the JMBG it is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. But what I'm saying is there was at least 32 per cent that had incomplete JMBGs. So at least 32 per cent of the 4.4 million you couldn't match.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. Not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At least through not through this identification?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is that if you have two numbers in two sources and both are incorrect but they are identical in the two sources it doesn't matter. If you have them you can match because they are all the same in the two sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the important thing about the marching of the census and the voters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The census material was used for the register of voters exactly as available from the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is not the case with many other sources that we used but in this particular case it was the big advantage we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know how many folks that were in Bosnia-Herzegovina chose not to register to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly, but it is estimated that 82 per cent registered to vote so 18 wouldn't register.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, and how many people?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the OSCE estimate, sorry, not mine. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, and how many people did not register to vote that were living outside of BiH?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is a difficult question, and I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I don't think anybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One last couple of questions, just another three, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And these are technical questions and I've just -- maybe you can help me out here. Dealing with Mostar, we know that after Dayton, Mostar became what is it six municipalities -- or eight municipalities; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And prior -- prior to Dayton had been one municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now when you -- and I believe you said something about bridging over during -- you tried to bridge over in order to figure out who was where and how many and from that determine how many failed to return or how many would have been "ethnically cleansed" or refugees or internally displaced persons; am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the bridging and I mentioned the term "bridging," "bridging system" in the context of the new municipalities. In order to be able to produce statistics for the new municipalities, a bridging system is needed that would link the small statistical areas within the Mostar, pre-war Mostar big municipalities with the eight new post-war Mostar municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And now, did you start your calculations from the census circles?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we -- I don't understand exactly what you mean here. Do you -- the question is whether we used the census data to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Did you start your calculations from the census circles? And I'm told that statistics have them and have sent you or should have sent you this information. What's a census circle? The lowest territorial unit by which population is registered.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, statistical area, or in the census it is enumeration area. This is how it called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay and how many are there for Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, for Mostar, very many. I wouldn't know exactly how many but we can check this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, well.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are very small areas, really, yes. The bridging system, I want to stress, I didn't make it myself. I received it from statistical authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Statistical authorities in BiH?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, at least, there's no sense in me questioning you on that because that's not your work product. That's somebody else --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my work product, it is the product of the statistical authority of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Very well, and did you double-check it to see, to make sure that it's accurate?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- what can I do is making maps and seeing how it works in practice. But I can't check in terms that I can go to Mostar --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why can't you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Area by area and check every statistical area and check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you can do a sample, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You could do a sample, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bridging system is an official table that comes from the statistical authority. This is not my task to challenge the bridging system somebody, a statistical authority, developed in Bosnia for their use in the country. It is something that comes to me and I use it. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that's all I have. I appreciate the extra time. Unfortunately, it would have been better to have two or three days, I could have gone at a slower pace. I want to thank you for coming here and testifying. And I want to again thank the Coric team for giving me the 30 minutes. I believe that Ms. Alaburic did have a question that she wished to put, and it was so -- rather technical and I was unable to articulate it, so perhaps if the Court could allow Ms. Alaburic two or three minutes. Otherwise I don't know what -- if she still thinks she needs the time but I'll leave it up to her.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today -- they say there is no interpretation so I'll start from the beginning. Today's question of His Honour Judge Antonetti recorded on pages 9 and 10 and the reply was as to the age of the victims as a possible criterion for establishing military or civilian status. The witness's reply was that that was one of the possible methods but that she did not use that method. I believe that based on table 18 and figure 6 from the report on those killed in Mostar we could establish numbers which might assist us in approximating ourselves to a reply to Judge Antonetti's question, and if I am allowed a few minutes I would like to explore this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I put my specific question, madam, can we agree that the population in Mostar in 1992 and 1993, and this includes East Mostar, was increased because of a large number of refugees? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree that it was increased but refugees I wouldn't think of refugees. These were people from other areas in Bosnia, so I wouldn't call them refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. We can speak of displaced persons. I'm not going into the legal definition of the people who arrived in East Mostar at the time, but tell me, among the people who arrived, whether they were internally displaced or refugees, can we agree that the vast majority of them were women, children, and elderly?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that really because I -- I wouldn't know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you any knowledge as to whether the arrival of displaced persons and/or refugees in a certain area, the number of military-able persons increases or does it, on the contrary, decrease as a proportion of the population?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if -- if it is just one population and one group decreases, the other one must increase, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. If we now look at your table 18 and figure 6, and you also mentioned this in the text, however, it's clear from figure 6 that there is a steep increase in persons over 65 years of age, both in the male and in the female populations. Although you did not analyse the causes of death for these people, would it be logical to conclude that regardless of sex, this information means that persons aged over 65 died of natural causes?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it would be a correct conclusion because this age group is larger than any other age group shown in this chart. It is just a very broad age group. All persons, 65 plus, are included in this group. So this is a category that is uncomparable with other categories. I would have to redo the chart and include all the ages starting 65 by five-year age groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, all your groups more or less cover five years, whereas the 65 plus age group can also include persons with a 30-year age span. The difference can be up to 30 years. Can we agree they can be from 65 to 95?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said. This is what I said, that the length of this interval is much larger than all other five-year age groups. Therefore, it is uncomparable with other age groups. Therefore, there is this jump you see in the chart because it is the aggregate age group. Large age interval.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In my opinion this is a group for which it might be logical to expect that a larger proportion of that group would die of natural causes, but I won't go into this any further. I wanted to explore this category of over 65 year olds. If we analyse the figures, however, we will see that the have a majority of those killed were in fact military-age men, and that is also your conclusion in the text that accompanies the table. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we were to exclude people aged over 65 for which it would be logical to expect that they died of natural causes to a greater extent than others, then the proportion of military-able men in the total population of those killed would be even greater. Would we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And if we analyse according to various criteria and calculate percentages, adding or leaving out certain categories of the population, we can conclude that there is a significantly greater proportion of military-age men who were killed in this population as compared women or men who were below or above military age. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If the number of military-age men who were killed is linked to the percentage of military-age men in the total population, which decreased because of the arrival of displaced persons or refugees, women, children, and elderly, then we can conclude that the proportion of military-age men who were killed in this same population is considerably greater than the proportion of women, children, and elderly, and men who were not of military age in that category of the population. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I need to read your statement because you -- you made some statements, but I -- I think I am -- I made it clear in the report that majority of these victims are men at military age. So there is no doubt about it, of course. But I think that age-based approach is just a different approach. We didn't use this approach. We used data-driven approach. So ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to point to this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, do you have any additional questions in redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have many questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have perhaps 15 minutes. I'm in your hands, Mr. President, if you prefer to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I also have questions for the witness. So theoretically we should take a break at 5.30 because we started at 4.00 at any rate. So let's take a break now and we will start with my questions and we will have 15 minutes for you. A 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions, but first I would like to be absolutely sure, and I'm asking a question to Mr. Karnavas. 1D 01658 which is demographics, is that what you talked to with -- talked about with the witness, this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are two articles that the witness wrote, but the one that I referred to was 1D 01658, as I recall. The other article you see in our bundle is 1657. That's just sort of an overview of -- of this conference. The title of that one is "Demography of Conflicts and Violence: An emerging field".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence mentioned two articles that you wrote, which I am finding out about during this hearing. One of this article was written with Mr. Jakub Bijak.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I read this article, I noted that some of your colleagues, demographer colleagues, made studies on missing persons or persons killed, and you actually write this in your article, especially in tables. For example, on page 197 there's a general chart giving the number of missing or killed persons between 1991 and 1995. As sources we have Mr. Bassiouni, an institution in Stockholm called SIPRI, a Mr. Boyle, Mr. Thomas, and Mr. Kenney [phoen]. So we find out that a great number of people have studied this topic of missing or killed people. Out of curiosity, I looked at your three reports because I was wondering whether you referred to other demographers in your report, and then I discover that you actually never made any comparisons with work that could have been made by other people like Mr. Bassiouni. So when studying your three reports it looks like you're the only expert in this field, but when reading this article we find out that there are other people who studied this problem, and on page 199, discover that these people, yourself and these people supported your work on different sources, notably sources from military reports of the ABiH. This was a question put to you by General Praljak as to whether you used the number of killed produced by the ABiH, and I note that in this article you referred to it, whereas you said that you did not have any access to these documents. So I'd like to understand why it is that in an article you quote this as one of your sources and why earlier you told us that you had no knowledge of ABiH archives regarding the number of people killed within the army of ABiH. Could you answer my question, please?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, question number one related to the overview of estimates of war-related deaths in Bosnia by others. I want to make clear that those other names in the table 2 on page 197 are not demographers. This is one -- just one of them was produced by researchers. The other ones come from totally different persons. I, actually, in the article criticise these estimates and some other locally made estimates for the lack of transparency and for unclear sources and some of them even for being politically motivated. I think when it comes to Bosnia then, indeed, it is hard to find transparent scientific estimates of the -- of the victim -- of the number of victims. Actually, the number we produced and published in this article with Jakub Bijak is one, is the probably first one of this sort. Well, why didn't I make references to the work of others in my three reports on Herceg-Bosna? Well, that is serious difference between the Herceg-Bosna studies and the study of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There has been a lot of interest in the number of victims in the Bosnian wars, that means the victims from Bosnia and Herzegovina as such, and many people produced these kind of numbers, both in the former Yugoslavia and outside it, including the commission by Cherif Bassiouni in the first place. When it comes to a small area like Herceg-Bosna it is hard to find comparable figures. Of course, I could have referred to certain figures I know but none of these figures could be of the same sort as our estimates. There is a figure by Edward Vulliamy, for instance, who speaks of 1.100 to 1.200 victims of the siege of East Mostar. Well, this number is in line with our number of killed persons. The more complete number of the persons killed. There are also some other estimates or, say, better -- well, I would call them estimates but non-scientific estimates by people from Mostar itself. I know that a person from the company that was responsible for burials and cleaning up the streets from the parties who was in charge of these kind of activities estimated the number of victims at 1.700 persons, but -- and of course there are a few others. There is a military estimate that is approximately 1.000, a little bit and -- 1.000 of victims. The military estimate, I mean coming from a military who served in the Bosnian army during the conflict. Well, I didn't refer to them because to me it's hard to refer to figures that are not entirely transparent in terms of methodology and in terms of sources. So this is the reason why. But there are such figures, definitely. But the figures I produced are -- can be justified in terms of sources, in terms of method, and in terms of deficiencies and in terms of coverage. The others would be much harder from this point of view. This is why. Regarding the military lists that I used for the estimate for Bosnia, exactly the same lists were used in this project in the reports I produced in this report -- in this case -- for this case. These are the same military lists of fallen soldiers and other military personnel, the same version, the same source, the ministries of the defence. Everything exactly the same. So I used -- I did use this source in my Mostar studies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have another question. Last week when Defence asked you on what basis you made your research, at one point in time it seemed that some figures had been given to you by Sarajevo, by an intelligence department which had provided figures on the number of killed and missing persons. And when I look at the article you wrote, which I mentioned earlier and which was presented by Mr. Karnavas, I note that you also made reference to a CIA report called "Military History of Yugoslavia." So this report from the CIA, which must probably be based on elements, I would like to know whether you read this article or whether the references you make in this article are purely formal. Did you read all the references included in the footnotes of the CIA report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly didn't read the entire report. It is a very considerable report. I did read parts of the report related to general history of the conflict but certainly not all of it. But at the same time because I read these parts I can't say this is a formal reference that I just gave for the sake of having a reference. Well, I was using it for historical -- for the introduction, for the history of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question now. Could the registrar please call up document 9837, figure 6 on page 20 of the English version. And on page 30 of the B/C/S version. Figure 6 gives us the distribution of victims according to age and sex. So we have two curves on the screen.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask, it is the report on the killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, the killed. It's gone. It's not on the screen any more. Figure 6 on page 20 of the English version, please. No, this is not it. It was the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe for the record the report on the killed is P 9835, not 9837. She may be looking at the wrong exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Well, in the document you gave us, Mr. Stringer, it's 9837.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then I apologise, Your Honour. It's -- I could be wrong, but I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's on the screen now. It's on the screen. It's on the screen on the B/C/S version, so we'll work with the B/C/S version. Witness, please, this is a chart giving the distribution of victims according to age. From 0 to 4, that's the first age, and then it ends up with 65 plus. In red we have the women, females, and in black the males, or the men. When looking at this -- these curves, we see peaks. We see that there's obviously a peak in the men killed in the 20 to 24, 25 to 29, 30 to 34, and 35 to 39 age ranges, and then it decreases. If there were only civilian victims, given that statistically normally there's as many men as women, the curve for men should be similar to the curve for women, but here we have a big difference between the men and the women. And one could draw from this that there's a peak because of the military victims. If there were only civilians who were killed, as women, then the two curves should be identical or very close to each other, or almost -- they should almost overlap, whereas here we have this peak. So how do you explain this peak in the number of killed men? Isn't because in the 20- to 40-year range there are a lot of men who are in uniform, who are military, and that's why we have so many men? And these men could very well be military. If these men were civilians, there the curve of -- there shouldn't be any discrepancies between the two curves between men and women, between the two genders. Could you please answer my question?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Well, first of all we don't know exactly how many were there, how many men, how many women in the population in East Mostar, but generally what Your Honour said about -- if the numbers would be the same, then the -- and -- then the age distribution of the victims should be largely similar. That is a correct observation. Well, it's important to remember that this particular chart is showing both civilians and militaries jointly. There is no distinction here. It is a combination of these two categories. These are all victims, the minimum number, 539. Well, it is obvious that a majority of victims are men at military age. Likely that many of them were military, simply speaking. How many? Well, we only have the estimate. We cannot say specifically by age how many because that is not possible in this particular case. Well, next thing I want to stress is that that in conflict situation is a result of as well not only military status, civilian military status, but also risk-taking behaviour. This is a very important factor. In populations in conflict, the weakest are usually saved from being exposed to risk. Women and children are saved by others, by men, who tend to take the risk, the higher risk behaviour on themselves. It is, of course, combat on the first place, but on the second place there are other behaviours, simple things; collecting food or water or wood for fire, these kind of things. So I believe that generally men are more exposed to risk in conflict situation. This is another factor. Not all of them are militaries. There will be always more men seen among the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but this chart, you know, on the 65 plus age range, this was a question that was asked by Defence, but here what is really strange is the mortality rate is higher for the 65 plus age range, and a number of women killed, there were 23 or 24, 25 women over 65 killed, and in that age range also there are about 40 men who were killed, and there both curves are almost identical except there's more men dying than women.
