But in the 65 plus age range the curve picks up. But you know women tend to live longer than men. So we have this age range 65 plus. Isn't it -- does it mean that when we see the age range 20 -- 20 to 50 age range. Couldn't that prove that there were a lot of military in the 20 to 50 age range?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't relate the peak for age group 65 plus with other peaks in these curves. Well, first of all these are not rates, not relative measures. These are just absolute numbers shown in this chart. As I noted earlier today, the 65 plus is a larger age group, larger then any other age group. That means it is to be expected that the number of victims in this age group is higher than in the, for instance, preceding age group, 60-64. I wouldn't pay too much attention to this because that is -- in order to have a better understanding of how many died at age 65 plus, it's really necessary to redo this chart and show the data by five-year age groups also after age 65. So my first explanation is this is a larger age group than all other age groups. So the biggest -- most likely not there, I'm pretty sure it's not there. If we would have redo -- redone this chart and also for this age group show five-year age intervals, there wouldn't be peak as such. Although, generally speaking, of course, mortality increases with age and is much higher at higher ages than at lower ages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one last question now. Mr. Karnavas asked you some questions about this, but I'm not quite satisfied with your answers. On the title of your report, document 9835, people wounded in relation to the siege of Mostar. The word "siege" that you use, is it the senior officials at the Prosecution that asked you to do that or did you come up with the title yourself? How did you come up with this title? Was it the OTP who told you to study the victims of the "siege," spelling this word out for you, or is it a demographer who said, "I will come up with this title and call it a siege"? So Mr. Karnavas asked you a few questions about that, but I would like more information on this.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. The Prosecution didn't tell me what title to give to -- to my reports. This is a title I gave to this reports. Why the siege? I have done a lot of work on the siege of Sarajevo, and I believe the idea of using the word "siege" comes from my work on Sarajevo, on the siege of Sarajevo. Well -- and in the case of Sarajevo work, I didn't use this term in any other way than in the context of the common use of this term. There is no special connotations that are behind using this term at all. This is how this episode of the war was often called in the media and in the reports of international observers, and this is how I ended using it, and this is the same reason that I used that term for my work on Mostar. I saw certain similarities between the two situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I saw Mr. Praljak getting up. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to take up too much time, but I have noted 18 concepts which have nothing to do with demography: Water, electricity, Ustasha, Orlovac, siege, narrow belt on the west side, cellar, old, generator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Another follow-up question. In the reports that you made on Sarajevo were they also called siege of Sarajevo? I haven't read those reports on Sarajevo, but did you use the same title, Siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The word "siege" was used in the title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have also a few questions. The first relates to the table, to this drawing we have seen a minute ago where we also have a peak with the age group around 30 of men. Do you have inkling, any idea of whether that could also at least partly, partly, be explained by a higher proportion of men in that age group in the whole population at the time?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't think I have any data that could be used to answer this question. Not in relation to the population in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your article you speak about samples and about the double mentions with -- Mr. Karnavas, I think it was, has interrogated you about that, and at one point the figure of 8.500 duplicated records is mentioned. Eight thousand five hundred related to which total?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, 4.4 million individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is that a figure which statistically has significance?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, just a few follow-up questions. You were asked a series of questions by counsel for Dr. Prlic about census data, guidelines made for how to incorporate data, procedures, deficiencies with the census data, and just is -- is all of this dealt with in Annex B3 of your report on the refugees and the internally displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is discussed at length in this annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And in particular, I just want to direct your attention to page 66 of that report. Sorry, 66 being the first page of Annex B3. And here you actually refer in the footnote to Nora Selimovic, who is the person I believe you talked about as having been the source of information you received.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to note that I actually asked for two reports, one from Nora Selimovic. In parallel, I also independently asked for another report from another person who was also involved in the preparation and conduct of the population census. I compared these two reports. I received both, compared, and included in this report just one because the consistency of these two reports was perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just a question or two about the article that Mr. Karnavas asked you about in the cross-examination. And again, just so we're clear, if I could direct you -- in fact, it was the President who directed you to page 199, the reference to military records of fallen soldiers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The references there military records BH government army, the ABiH; and then VRS; and then thirdly HVO, are those in fact the records that you did rely on in part in making this report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked a few questions on cross-examination about whether the census had been officially completed or -- or approved; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the census, just to sort of take one step back from it, we've been talking about population data from the census; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether this census or censuses in general, whether this census was intended to assemble information or data about other things apart strictly from census data?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, population was just one part of it. It was also a census on households, on dwellings and agricultural farms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, as between those different groupings what level of completion did the population data attain that you've based your report on?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in terms of data checks, logical checks, the population was -- had achieved, had achieved the highest level of attention and success. That means this particular part of the census data has been practically finished and publications were made in relation to publications, several publications by authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and also in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were asked about whatever data or information may have been available to you regarding pre-conflict patterns of voluntary migration within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just referring to page 10 of your report. The very last paragraph at the bottom of that page, page 10. Moving down to the fourth line you say: "Pre-conflict internal migration in Bosnia and Herzegovina was negligible," and then you talk about usual causes of internal migration. Could you just briefly comment on what one would expect in terms of normal patterns and numbers as compared to the numbers that you arrive at in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned earlier today that I tried to find data on internal migration, in particular for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I contacted the statistical authority in Sarajevo and requested what kind of data they had. They sent me a bulletin, statistical bulletin number 271 that I also had in my office, and I studied data from this bulletin. This data comes from the 1991 population census and shows the internal migration and external migration at the outbreak of the conflict. That means in 1991. I have extracted the relevant data and made a table with this data. I have the table with me. I also placed the data on internal migration in the context of the census population in Herceg-Bosna municipalities and calculated some rates. These rates I obtained confirm what is in the report and confirm that the internal migration was negligible, and at that time also the external migration from Herceg-Bosna to other countries was also negligible practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have this publication registered with the evidence unit, and also the table I made and I can submit this material if --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's available if the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's available, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- wants it. Witness, just one last question on that point then. Can you comment briefly on your assessment or your observation in terms of the scale, the level of migration pre-conflict as compared to the data then that you've come up with based on the post-conflict migration?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may just very briefly. I don't object to hearing the answer. However, clearly, and I assume Mr. Stringer did not have any contact with the witness and this is the witness's own doing on her own, but certainly this information was not provided to us. And if you're going to go -- if the Prosecution wishes to go into that area, one, it is outside the scope in the sense that now we're going to specific data that was looked at by the demographer on her own over the weekend and has not been made available to the Defence. While I do not object to the Prosecutor opening up his direct examination in this area, it may require for us at some other point to request for the witness to come back to -- to provide additional questions -- provide additional answers in relation to this particular topic because of the new information that's being -- that we are not -- was not made available to us by the -- by the expert. So, again, I don't want to appear that they were trying to keep it out, but I think it's only fair that if it becomes necessary for us to go to question further, I certainly am not prepared today. I would like some time and I would give the Court notice and the witness is in The Hague so it's not going to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, Mr. Stringer, you want the witness to talk to you about migration after the conflict, that is to say, after the Dayton agreements and after the war. And Mr. Karnavas, if I'm not mistaken, deems that this is not information that they had and therefore he would like to object to your question. Am I mistaken? I don't know if I'm mistaken, but, Mr. Stringer, you wanted to put this question to the witness as to how did people move after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... No, not just that, Mr. President. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, not only that but that as well, the migration patterns; right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me perhaps re-ask the question because I'm trying to tie this into something that is found in the witness's report and simply ask her to elaborate on that. And let me say that certainly I've not had any contact whatsoever with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may then rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Again, just drawing your attention, Witness, to this last paragraph on page 10. You refer to minimal internal migration. Could you elaborate on that? What was the basis for that statement? And then how -- what does that tell you about the level of migration that you determined post-conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, again I don't mean to be obstreperous but now we have the witness looking at a piece -- at a chart that was generated that is not being that is not part of the question. And I know Mr. Stringer is an honourable man and didn't contact, but -- and Mr. Stringer is doing correct redirect by going back to the -- the report which we all have, but if the witness is going to be looking at charts she prepared that is not available to the Defence, I would object to that. And Mr. Stringer has not asked her to look at that but she has been looking at that. So I would ask the witness to kindly put aside anything that she has that is not part of her report and just focus on Mr. Stringer's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, if I'm not mistaken, and usually I have a good memory, at some point, and I don't have the transcript before me, but didn't you say that you and your staff studied documents stemming from the relocation commission of the people who were coming back and that you examined the charts of that commission? Is that what you said earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly what the relocation commission is. I did study some figures by UNHCR, but the whole discussion now is about the issue of pre-war internal migration in Bosnia, pre-war internal migration in Bosnia, in order to have some context for the figures on internal migration, displaced persons, and refugees produced in my report. And I have collected these figures, and I looked at the figures, and I can only say that I fully stand behind my statement from the report that before the conflict, before the conflict, as seen from the data available in the 1991 census, the internal migration in this particular region of Bosnia is negligible. And not only internal but also external. And I can confirm this if Your Honours and everybody else wishes by providing additional analysis, but I -- for now I can only say this. It has all been confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, but Mr. Stringer wanted to talk about the migration patterns post-conflict. Did you study that as well? In other words, how many people came back to live in their former houses, domiciles? How many people came back to their dwellings from a foreign country? Did you study that? It does not -- it's not included in your report, but just as a curiosity point. Did you study that particular post-migration pattern, the return of these people back to their dwellings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on several occasions I looked at UNHCR statistics on returns and on displaced persons and refugees as well. Well, I don't think it is possible to obtain statistics, UNHCR statistics, for such a small region as Herceg-Bosna that is available. We can speak of these figures for the entire country, Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I don't think we can have these statistics for comparative purposes for the eight municipalities studied in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Prlic wanted to say something. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] I'd like to say something to redirect, a question put by Mr. Stringer and also linked to Ms. Nora Selimovic, and I found a piece of information there that I consider could be of interest. On page 76 of this report the last two lines read as follows, and what is referred to is her data and her curriculum vitae. [In English] "In October 1998 after the creation of the state agency for statistics in Bosnia and Herzegovina, she commenced working in this institution. She is still employed there at present." [Interpretation] This sentence reminded me of the fact that I was the person who adopted the law on the statistical office at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because at that time in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were just three ministries. So in the space of time between 1992 to 1998, I don't know which institution existed, who checked the data, and who published the data. I also know that in the budget for Bosnia-Herzegovina, not for 1996 or 1997 did there exist an area of the existence of the statistical institute at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, reference to that. So I don't know who published that data and who verified that data.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I answer this? Well, the republican statistical office has always been in Sarajevo at exactly the same as before April 1992. This is the statistical authority who processed the census data and who submitted to the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina reports on the conduct of the census. The reports were required by the census law to be provided by the end of March for the year, for preceding year, and at least three such reports were submitted. I have copies of this report. If required, I can submit copies. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] May I just say that that does not answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, Mr. Prlic asked you a question. Would you be able to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the statistical office of the Federation of Bosnia And Herzegovina that processed the census data. The state agency is an umbrella that covers two statistical authorities; one in the federation and one in Republika Srpska. They themselves didn't have anything to do with the data from the census as such. So the federal authority, the federal statistical authority was the one that processed the census data and made publications. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Of course I'm not satisfied with the answer because part of the state which is half a state cannot deal with information that relates to the state as whole and I think the question steps outside the limits of this examination, but let's stay with what has been recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, and just for the sake of clarity, Your Honour, the witness indicated federation and then she said federal. Now, because there is the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I mean sometimes lawyers and Judges have confused it when they hear federal, at least in my context it's state. So if the witness could elaborate. Is there -- how is she using this term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm using this as the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record, Ms. Winner has called up a part of the transcript from last week, and a question from Judge Trechsel, which I think Mr. Karnavas referred to earlier. Judge Trechsel asked, said: "I wanted to ask you whether you have, whether you have science -- whether your science has any figures on what a normal migration is in given area and over a period of six, seven years." And then the witness said, "Not that I have these kind of figures at hand now, but I believe the figures on normal migration in the region of the former Yugoslavia do exist, and for reference purposes, I certainly can look for those figures and I can provide this Chamber with those figures for comparison." And so it's my impression that the witness then went and found those figures and has brought them back should the Trial Chamber wish to see those today. That's just for the record, and I have only one or two questions left, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The first is, Witness, whether you know if in fact the census data, the census figures from Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1991, whether they were published by any authorities outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, certainly. The -- Croatia published the census data, the ethnic composition by settlements. And Mr. Praljak was using this publication during his cross-examination. This includes beautiful maps for every municipality showing the composition in settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the last issue, and I'm going to ask if the technical people could put up the PowerPoint on the screens. I've just got one slide that I'd like to ask the witness to comment on. It's one that we skipped over in her direct in order to move more quickly. But, Witness, today and I believe last week, during the course of your testimony the word "extrapolation" was used, and I know that this applies not just to this specific example but to others as well. This is table 16 from your report on the wounded people in East Mostar. And if you could with this table perhaps explain to us the manner of extrapolation that you've referred to, specifically how the percentages then were applied from smaller numbers to larger numbers.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is a table that contains information about causes, distribution of victims by cause of wounding. In the first column the overall total is 5.867 of which 2.000, approximately 2.500 are cases with diagnosis available and explicitly reported in the hospital books, and there is a number of unknown cases. This is the 2.844, 2.844.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, now let me just jump in there. When it says unknown, what exactly are you talking about here when you say unknown?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The diagnosis is not reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So in that book we looked at nothing's written. It doesn't say vulnus explosiva or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. This is unavailable. This is unknown. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just to continue with that because some questions came out suggesting that the doctor didn't know what was the nature of the wound and I wanted to clarify between whether the doctor -- whether it was unknown because the doctor didn't know or whether this was unknown to you because it wasn't in the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Just for the sake of the record, I object. I think the Prosecutor misunderstood, but I don't think anyone made that suggestion, and I think that in fairness to the Defence the question should be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just wanting to make a hundred per cent sure. If I misunderstood, then I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ask a non-leading question and you'll get the answer. We can move on, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for that ruling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So there is a number of cases with unknown diagnosis. Unknown means not reported in the books. And in this table we present minimum numbers in the first -- in the first column in the table. And there is a percentage distribution in the next column. In the calculation of the percentages two categories have been skipped. This is the 2.844 unknowns and 474 cases from missing pages or too incomplete to include in the analysis. Well, in the next column there is an estimated value of wounded persons by the same categories of wounding. Below the table there is a formula that explains how the calculation was made. The calculation takes, as a beginning, the minimum numbers of reported cases. For instance if we take shelling as an example, there were 2.088 cases of victims -- wounded persons of whom we know these were victims of shelling. So we take this as the first component of the estimate and as the second component we take a percentage of the unknowns. The per cent that is given in the second column of the table. 81.9 per cent are the cases of shelling. So we simply take the 81.9 per cent out of 2.844 and added to the minimum numbers observed in the source. And as a result of this procedure we have the estimated value of victims or number of victims of shelling which is 4.418. The percentage distribution remains the same. In the last part of the table we give confidence intervals of this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that the 81.9 per cent, which is known from the observed -- from those records that you could see, you simply applied that same percentage then to the number of unknowns, which were 2.844?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what was done consequently in all these estimations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, we just ended your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to testify at the request of the OTP. Thank you for testifying, therefore, and thank you for bringing your comments to the reports that you've drafted. No, no. So I would like to ask the usher to escort you out of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, for the rest of the week we don't have any other witnesses because it was not possible to have a witness, and therefore there won't be a hearing tomorrow, no hearings on Wednesday, nor on Thursday. Now, next week we have a witness. I'm not going to give the witness's name because I don't know if it is a protected witness or not, but it's a witness who is scheduled for four days, Monday through Thursday. The legal officer will send you the information with regard to the time, the division of time, because I can't tell you that now since the witness is here for the first -- for four days, the first day will be dedicated to the Prosecution, and the day after as well, and the Defence will probably have two or two days and a half to cross-examine this witness. This is what I wanted to tell you. And if there are no further questions, I will therefore adjourn this hearing and we will see each other next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of September, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
